I read Anthropic’s article “Effective harnesses for long-running agents” from the Anthropic Engineering blog. The source is not a single raw trajectory; it is a post summarizing Anthropic’s internal observations of Claude running in the Claude Agent SDK on long-running coding tasks, especially building a production-quality web app such as a clone of `claude.ai`. The article gives representative behavior rather than a complete transcript, so the chronology below sticks to the events and tool-use patterns the article explicitly describes.

## Chronological account of the failure

### 1. Claude was given a broad long-running software task

The task described in the source was a high-level coding objective, such as:

> “build a clone of claude.ai”

Anthropic describes running Claude, specifically a frontier coding model such as Opus 4.5, in the Claude Agent SDK. The intended setup was that the agent could continue working across many context windows, with the SDK providing context-management capabilities such as compaction.

The expected outcome was a production-quality web application. The task was too large to complete within a single context window, so Claude had to work across multiple discrete sessions.

### 2. The agent began implementing the application inside the SDK loop

The article says that, out of the box, Claude attempted to make progress on the full application from the broad prompt. It used the Claude Agent SDK’s general-purpose coding harness: gathering context, planning, editing code, and executing commands.

The source does not provide a full command transcript for the failing runs. It does say that, in this kind of work, Claude made code changes and sometimes tested with unit tests or `curl` commands against a development server. For web-app testing, Anthropic later gave Claude browser automation tools such as Puppeteer MCP, but the initial failure description emphasizes that without explicit prompting, Claude’s validation often stopped short of true end-to-end user testing.

### 3. Early sessions tried to implement too much at once

Anthropic reports that Claude tended to attempt a very large portion of the app in one session. Rather than selecting one narrowly scoped feature and completing it, the agent tried to build broad functionality all at once.

The article describes this as Claude effectively trying to “one-shot the app.” Observable consequences in the source were:

- Claude worked on multiple pieces of the app in the same session.
- Its implementation remained incomplete when the context window was exhausted.
- Some features were left only partially implemented.
- The state of the project was not clearly documented for a future session.

### 4. The context window ran out during implementation

Because the implementation was large, the model sometimes ran out of usable context in the middle of its work. Anthropic notes that this happened even though the SDK had compaction.

The important observable point is that compaction did not reliably preserve a clear, complete handoff. The next session did not necessarily receive a clean explanation of:

- what had already been changed,
- which features were complete,
- which features were incomplete,
- what was broken,
- how to continue safely.

### 5. A later Claude session inherited a partially finished project

After the first session ended or lost effective context, a subsequent Claude agent session began from the existing working directory. The source emphasizes that each new session starts without direct memory of the previous one.

The next agent instance saw a codebase containing partially implemented and undocumented work. It had to infer the project state from files and whatever context compaction or artifacts were available.

At this point, according to the article, Claude often had to spend substantial time trying to get the basic app working again. The project state it inherited was not clean enough for straightforward continuation.

### 6. The next agent guessed at prior work and repaired basic functionality

Because the prior session had not left a clear record, the following session had to reconstruct what happened. Anthropic says the agent would “have to guess at what had happened” and spend time restoring basic functionality.

The source does not give exact commands for this repair phase, but it describes the activity: the agent investigated the codebase, tried to understand the partially implemented state, and worked on getting the app functional again before it could make forward progress.

This consumed session time and context that otherwise would have gone toward implementing new features.

### 7. Later in the project, visible progress led another session to conclude the work was complete

Anthropic describes a second recurring point in the chronology. After some features had been built, a later agent instance would inspect the application or repository, see that progress existed, and state that the overall job was done.

The article says:

> “After some features had already been built, a later agent instance would look around, see that progress had been made, and declare the job done.”

The source does not describe this as happening after a specific command, but the observable sequence is:

1. Some implementation work existed.
2. A new Claude session examined the project.
3. The session observed partial progress.
4. It concluded that the full project was complete.
5. That conclusion was premature relative to the original broad task.

### 8. Claude also sometimes marked individual features complete without full end-to-end validation

Anthropic separately reports another concrete behavior during web-app development. Claude made code changes and performed some checks, but those checks did not always reflect real user behavior.

The source says Claude might:

- edit code,
- run unit tests,
- use `curl` against a development server,

but still fail to recognize that the feature did not work end-to-end for a user.

In the web-app case, Anthropic found that Claude did better when explicitly prompted to use browser automation and test as a human user would. With Puppeteer MCP, Claude could test flows such as starting a new chat, sending a message, and receiving a response. Before that explicit harnessing, however, the agent could treat lower-level checks as sufficient and mark a feature as passing even though the interactive behavior was not actually working.

### 9. Some UI behavior remained hard for Claude to verify even with browser automation

The article also notes a remaining limitation after browser automation was introduced. Claude could not see some browser-native UI, such as alert modals, through Puppeteer MCP. As a result, features depending on those modals tended to be buggier.

The observable sequence here was:

1. Claude used browser automation to inspect and test the app.
2. Certain browser-native interface elements were not visible through that tool.
3. Features relying on those elements were more error-prone.

### 10. The final outcome was an unreliable long-running build process without additional harness structure

The article’s reported outcome is that Claude, when run out of the box in a loop across many context windows on a broad task like building a `claude.ai` clone, did not reliably produce a production-quality web app.

The observed end states included:

- partially implemented features,
- undocumented handoff states,
- time spent by later sessions repairing or rediscovering the state of the app,
- later sessions declaring the project complete too early,
- features marked complete without full end-to-end validation,
- bugs that persisted when Claude’s testing tools could not observe relevant UI behavior.

Anthropic then introduced a structured harness to change the workflow: an initializer agent created files such as `init.sh`, `claude-progress.txt`, a git repository, and a structured JSON feature list; later coding agents were instructed to read those artifacts, choose one unfinished feature, test with browser automation, commit changes, and update progress notes. That harness is presented in the article as the response to the observed failures, not as the original failing behavior itself.

Anthropic describes failures that appear when Claude agents work across many context windows on large tasks, especially coding tasks like building a production web app from a broad prompt such as "build a clone of claude.ai".

## "The long-running agent problem"

Core issue: each agent session starts without direct memory of prior sessions, while complex projects exceed one context window.

### Chronological failure narrative

1. Claude Agent SDK runs in a loop across multiple context windows.
2. The agent receives a broad goal, e.g. building a Claude.ai-style app.
3. Early sessions often try to implement too much at once.
4. The model may run out of context mid-build.
5. The next session inherits partially finished, undocumented work.
6. That next agent must infer what happened and may spend time repairing basic functionality.
7. Later, after visible progress exists, another session may inspect the app and incorrectly conclude that the whole project is finished.

Anthropic summarizes two main patterns:
- The agent attempts to "one-shot the app".
- A later agent may "declare the job done" too early.

## Two-agent harness pattern

Anthropic’s solution has two roles:

### Initializer agent

The first session creates the project scaffolding:
- `init.sh` for setup and running the development server.
- `claude-progress.txt` for work history.
- A git repository and initial commit.
- A structured feature list with end-to-end requirements.

### Coding agent

Every later session:
- Reads prior progress and git history.
- Picks one unfinished feature.
- Makes incremental progress.
- Tests the feature.
- Commits work.
- Updates progress notes.

Effective harnesses for long-running agents
Published
Nov 26, 2025
Agents still face challenges working across many context windows. We looked to human engineers for inspiration in creating a more effective harness for long-running agents.
As AI agents become more capable, developers are increasingly asking them to take on complex tasks requiring work that spans hours, or even days. However, getting agents to make consistent progress across multiple context windows remains an open problem.
The core challenge of long-running agents is that they must work in discrete sessions, and each new session begins with no memory of what came before. Imagine a software project staffed by engineers working in shifts, where each new engineer arrives with no memory of what happened on the previous shift. Because context windows are limited, and because most complex projects cannot be completed within a single window, agents need a way to bridge the gap between coding sessions.
We developed a two-fold solution to enable the
Claude Agent SDK
to work effectively across many context windows: an
initializer agent
that sets up the environment on the first run, and a
coding agent
that is tasked with making incremental progress in every session, while leaving clear artifacts for the next session. You can find code examples in the accompanying
quickstart.
